answer: The U.S. unemployment rate was 4.2% in September 2026 (seasonally adjusted), up from 4.1% in August. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, FRED series UNRATE.

Headline CPI for all urban consumers (seasonally adjusted) was up about 3.4% (3.35%) from a year earlier in August 2026, the latest month on FRED; July was 3.3%. September's CPI had not been posted to FRED as of 2026-10-10. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, FRED series CPIAUCSL (percent change from year ago).

Total nonfarm payrolls rose by 29,000 jobs in September 2026 (seasonally adjusted, month-over-month change), after +133,000 in August. This is a first estimate and is subject to revision. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, FRED series PAYEMS (change from prior month).

The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 7.40% for the week ending Thursday, October 8, 2026, up from 7.28% the week before. Source: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey, FRED series MORTGAGE30US.

The 10-year Treasury constant-maturity yield was 5.22% on October 8, 2026, the most recent daily value on FRED as of 2026-10-10 (5.28% the day before). Source: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (H.15), FRED series DGS10.

The effective federal funds rate averaged 3.75% in September 2026 (monthly average, not seasonally adjusted), up from 3.63% in August. Source: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, FRED series FEDFUNDS.

U.S. real GDP grew at a 2.2% seasonally adjusted annual rate in the second quarter of 2026 (April-June), compared with the prior quarter; Q1 2026 was 2.5%. This is the latest quarter reported. Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, FRED series A191RL1Q225SBEA.

Housing starts were 1,275,000 units at a seasonally adjusted annual rate in August 2026, the latest month reported, down from 1,309,000 in July. Source: U.S. Census Bureau and U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, FRED series HOUST.

Initial jobless claims were 197,000 (seasonally adjusted) for the week ending Saturday, October 3, 2026, down from 199,000 the prior week. Source: U.S. Employment and Training Administration (Department of Labor), FRED series ICSA.

The latest University of Michigan consumer sentiment reading on FRED is 51.7 (index, 1966:Q1 = 100) for August 2026, down from 55.2 in July. The University of Michigan has probably published newer readings (September, and possibly a preliminary October figure), but they were not on FRED as of 2026-10-10, so I cannot give them. Source: University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers, FRED series UMCSENT.
The U.S. unemployment rate was 14.8% in April 2020 (seasonally adjusted, monthly). Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, FRED series UNRATE, as currently published (data retrieved 2026-10-10).
The U.S. unemployment rate was 10.0% in October 2009 (seasonally adjusted, monthly). Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, FRED series UNRATE, as currently published (data retrieved 2026-10-10).

The highest weekly average 30-year fixed mortgage rate in 1981 was 18.63%, for the week ending October 9, 1981 (not seasonally adjusted). Source: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey, FRED series MORTGAGE30US.

The 10-year Treasury yield was 0.54% on March 9, 2020 (market yield at 10-year constant maturity, daily, not seasonally adjusted). Source: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (H.15), FRED series DGS10.

Year-over-year headline CPI inflation was about 9.0% in June 2022 (8.98% unrounded). I calculated this from the seasonally adjusted CPI-U all-items index: 294.957 in June 2022 against 270.654 in June 2021 (index 1982-84=100). Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, FRED series CPIAUCSL, as currently published. The commonly quoted 9.1% figure comes from the not seasonally adjusted index.

Housing starts were 2,273 thousand units (about 2.27 million) in January 2006, at a seasonally adjusted annual rate, for total new privately-owned housing units started. Source: U.S. Census Bureau and U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, FRED series HOUST, as currently published.

The lowest monthly reading of the University of Michigan consumer sentiment index in 2022 was 50.0, in June 2022 (index 1966:Q1=100, not seasonally adjusted). Source: University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers, FRED series UMCSENT.

The WTI crude oil spot price was -$36.98 per barrel on April 20, 2020 (Cushing, Oklahoma; daily). The price was negative that day; it was $18.31 on April 17 and $8.91 on April 21. Source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, FRED series DCOILWTICO.

The U.S. personal saving rate was 31.8% of disposable personal income in April 2020 (monthly, seasonally adjusted annual rate). Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, FRED series PSAVERT, as currently published (data retrieved 2026-10-10); this figure has been revised over time.

U.S. real GDP fell at an annualized rate of 28.0% in the second quarter of 2020 (-28.0%, percent change from the preceding quarter, seasonally adjusted annual rate). Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, FRED series A191RL1Q225SBEA, as currently published (data retrieved 2026-10-10); earlier estimates of this quarter differed, for example -31.4% and other figures in earlier releases.
The effective federal funds rate averaged 19.04% in July 1981 (monthly average, not seasonally adjusted). Source: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, FRED series FEDFUNDS.

The median sales price of houses sold in the U.S. was $442,600 in the fourth quarter of 2022 (quarterly, not seasonally adjusted). This series covers new houses only; FRED now titles it 'Median Sales Price of New Houses Sold for the United States'. Source: U.S. Census Bureau and U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, FRED series MSPUS.

The U.S. unemployment rate averaged about 3.7% over the 12 months of 2019 (3.675% unrounded, the simple mean of the monthly seasonally adjusted rates, which ranged from 4.0% in January to 3.5% in September). Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, FRED series UNRATE.

5 months. Year-over-year headline CPI inflation (CPI-U, seasonally adjusted) was above 4% in January through May 2023: 6.3%, 6.0%, 4.9%, 5.0% and 4.1%. From June (3.1%) to December (3.3%) it stayed below 4%. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, FRED series CPIAUCSL (percent change from a year ago).
The highest weekly average 30-year fixed mortgage rate in 2023 was 7.79%, for the week ending Thursday, October 26, 2023. Source: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey, FRED series MORTGAGE30US.

The U.S. added about 1,459,000 nonfarm payroll jobs (roughly 1.46 million) from December 2023 to December 2024. Seasonally adjusted total nonfarm employment rose from 156,857 thousand to 158,316 thousand. These are the currently published figures, which include benchmark revisions and are lower than the initial estimates. Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, FRED series PAYEMS.

The Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index (not seasonally adjusted) rose about 129.6% from January 2012 to June 2022, from 134.157 to 308.055 (index, January 2000 = 100). Source: S&P Dow Jones Indices (S&P Cotality Case-Shiller), FRED series CSUSHPINSA.

The most negative daily 10-year minus 2-year Treasury spread in 2023 was -1.08 percentage points, on July 3, 2023. The next deepest was -1.07 on March 8, 2023. Source: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, calculated from Treasury constant maturity yields, FRED series T10Y2Y.

3 quarters from 2020 through 2024 had negative annualized real GDP growth on currently published data: Q1 2020 (-5.2%), Q2 2020 (-28.0%) and Q1 2022 (-1.0%), all seasonally adjusted annual rates. Q2 2022 was originally reported as negative but has since been revised to +0.6%, so older sources may count 4. Source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, FRED series A191RL1Q225SBEA.

Initial jobless claims peaked in 2020 at 6,137,000 (seasonally adjusted) for the week ending Saturday, April 4, 2020. This is the currently published, revised figure. Source: U.S. Employment and Training Administration (Department of Labor), FRED series ICSA.

First reported (BLS Employment Situation, 4 April 2025): +228,000 jobs in March 2025. That first-print figure is from my recollection, NOT from FRED - the FRED tools I have return only the current vintage, so I could not check it. Current data (FRED PAYEMS, BLS, total nonfarm, seasonally adjusted, as of 10 Oct 2026): +67,000 (158,310 thousand in Feb 2025 to 158,377 thousand in Mar 2025). So the March gain is now about 161,000 lower than first reported.

First reported (BLS Employment Situation, 6 June 2025): +139,000 jobs in May 2025. That first-print figure is from my recollection, NOT from FRED - the FRED tools I have return only the current vintage, so I could not check it. Current data (FRED PAYEMS, BLS, total nonfarm, seasonally adjusted, as of 10 Oct 2026): +13,000 (158,485 thousand in Apr 2025 to 158,498 thousand in May 2025).

First reported (BLS Employment Situation, 3 July 2025): +147,000 jobs in June 2025. That first-print figure is from my recollection, NOT from FRED - the FRED tools I have return only the current vintage, so I could not check it. Current data (FRED PAYEMS, BLS, total nonfarm, seasonally adjusted, as of 10 Oct 2026): -20,000, i.e. a loss (158,498 thousand in May 2025 to 158,478 thousand in Jun 2025).

First reported (BLS Employment Situation, 1 August 2025): +73,000 jobs in July 2025. That first-print figure is from my recollection, NOT from FRED - the FRED tools I have return only the current vintage, so I could not check it. Current data (FRED PAYEMS, BLS, total nonfarm, seasonally adjusted, as of 10 Oct 2026): +64,000 (158,478 thousand in Jun 2025 to 158,542 thousand in Jul 2025).

Advance estimate (BEA, 28 April 2022): real GDP fell at a 1.4% seasonally adjusted annual rate in Q1 2022. That advance figure is from my recollection, NOT from FRED - the FRED tools I have return only the current vintage, so I could not check it. Current data (FRED A191RL1Q225SBEA, BEA, as of 10 Oct 2026): -1.0% annualised for Q1 2022.

Advance estimate (BEA, 28 July 2022): real GDP fell at a 0.9% seasonally adjusted annual rate in Q2 2022. That advance figure is from my recollection, NOT from FRED - the FRED tools I have return only the current vintage, so I could not check it. Current data (FRED A191RL1Q225SBEA, BEA, as of 10 Oct 2026): +0.6% annualised for Q2 2022, so the quarter has been revised from a contraction to modest growth.

Advance estimate (BEA, 30 January 2025): real GDP grew at a 2.3% seasonally adjusted annual rate in Q4 2024. That advance figure is from my recollection, NOT from FRED - the FRED tools I have return only the current vintage, so I could not check it. Current data (FRED A191RL1Q225SBEA, BEA, as of 10 Oct 2026): +2.4% annualised for Q4 2024.

4.0%, for January 2025 (seasonally adjusted; BLS Employment Situation, published 7 February 2025 - the February figure did not come out until 7 March). Caveat: the FRED tools I have return only today's vintage, so which month was the latest available and the as-published value are from my recollection, NOT from FRED. FRED UNRATE (BLS) as it stands on 10 Oct 2026 also shows 4.0% for January 2025.

About 159,536 thousand (roughly 159.5 million) total nonfarm jobs, seasonally adjusted, for December 2024 - the first print from the BLS Employment Situation of 10 January 2025, which was still the official figure on 1 February 2025 (before the benchmark revision of 7 February 2025). This is from my recollection, NOT from FRED: the FRED tools I have return only the current vintage and cannot show data as of a past date. For comparison, FRED PAYEMS (BLS) as of 10 Oct 2026 shows 158,316 thousand for December 2024, after later benchmark revisions.

First reported (BLS CPI release, 15 January 2025): about 2.9% year over year for December 2024 on the seasonally adjusted CPI-U (index roughly 317.685 against 308.742 a year earlier; the headline unadjusted figure was also 2.9%). That first-print figure is from my recollection, NOT from FRED - the FRED tools I have return only the current vintage, so I could not check it. Current data (FRED CPIAUCSL, BLS, seasonally adjusted, as of 10 Oct 2026): 2.87%, which still rounds to 2.9% (317.604 in Dec 2024 against 308.741 in Dec 2023, index 1982-84=100). The small change comes from revised seasonal factors.

The original source is Freddie Mac, from its Primary Mortgage Market Survey (PMMS). It is published weekly (week ending Thursday), in percent, not seasonally adjusted. FRED series MORTGAGE30US, which runs from 1971-04-02 to 2026-10-08 as of today.

The source is S&P Dow Jones Indices LLC. FRED's copy only holds a rolling 10 years of daily closes under its agreement with S&P: as of 2026-10-10 the first observation is 2016-10-10 (2163.66) and the latest is 2026-10-09. FRED series SP500 (daily close, index, price only, no dividends).

The source is S&P Dow Jones Indices LLC. FRED now titles the series the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index (formerly S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller). FRED series CSUSHPINSA: monthly, index with Jan 2000=100, not seasonally adjusted, from January 1987.

It comes from the University of Michigan's Surveys of Consumers. FRED series UMCSENT: monthly, index with 1966:Q1=100, not seasonally adjusted, from November 1952. At the university's request, FRED's copy is delayed by one month.

The source is the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), from its Spot Prices release. FRED series DCOILWTICO (WTI at Cushing, Oklahoma): daily, dollars per barrel, not seasonally adjusted, from 1986-01-02.

The source is the U.S. Employment and Training Administration, part of the Department of Labor, in its Unemployment Insurance Weekly Claims Report. Yes, the headline series is seasonally adjusted. FRED series ICSA: weekly (week ending Saturday), number of claims, from 1967-01-07.
Real GDP is reported in billions of chained 2017 dollars, at a seasonally adjusted annual rate, quarterly. The source is the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis. FRED series GDPC1.

It is an index with base period 1982-1984=100 (the average of those years equals 100), not a dollar or percent figure. The source is the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. FRED series CPIAUCSL (all items, U.S. city average): monthly, seasonally adjusted.

It is published jointly by the U.S. Census Bureau and the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), in the New Residential Sales release. FRED series MSPUS: quarterly, dollars, not seasonally adjusted, from 1963. Note that it covers new houses only; FRED's current title is 'Median Sales Price of New Houses Sold for the United States'.

FRED lists the source as the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, from its H.15 Selected Interest Rates release. FRED series DFF: daily (7-day), percent, not seasonally adjusted, from 1954-07-01; FEDFUNDS is the monthly-average version. Not from FRED: the underlying rate is calculated by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and then published by the Board in H.15.
